Messages.Author: Steve Wampler
Messages.Body:
Emmanuel Martin wrote:
>
> As I am not very used with high level playing, I would like some
> help about a few decks. Thanks for "healing" them.
>
> Gangrel control deck
>
>The objective is to neutralize your predator then start bleeding your
> preys for one.

A very difficult concept to win with. Usually the best you can hope for
with an intercept deck is to get your predators killed one at a time,
then be the last man standing and win 2 VPs to everyone else's 1, and
even that isn't terribly easy.

>
>
> 4 Camille
> 4 Raven
> 4 Gitane St Claire

Um... I hate to have to be the one to tell you, but Camille and Raven
are officially the same card so you really only have two vampires in
this crypt. I do approve of the strategy you were trying for here (I
used a similar tact with my Ravnos intercept deck), but I would use at
least four different vampires. With four each of three you run the
(admittedly slight) risk of drawing all four of one of them. With three
of four you always get at least two and quite often (someone who's
better than me at math can figure out the exact percentage) get three.
Four is much rarer, but since you use mostly medium-large vamps that
have all the disciplines you need, you really don't want to pay for four
vampires anyway.
I suggest that you use 3 Camille (could be Raven, but Camille is way
hotter), 3 Gitane St. Clair, 3 Badger and 3 Bear Paw. You might also
consider adding Gunther, Beast Lord, Caitlin and Monique and use auspex
to beef up your intercept, but you won't rally need to do this if you
don't play in an environment with heavy stealth.

> Master cards 15
>
> 3 Animalism

Obviously, the number of Animalism cards you need depends on the crypt
you decide to use. You will always need some because all your vamps
need to be able to play cat's guidance at superior. If you go for the
auspex angle you will also want to add some skill cards for that.

> 1 Barrens
> 2 KRCG News Radio
> 1 Zoo Hunting Ground
> 1 Eco terrorists (a pretty but rare card)

I'd probably play with two of each of these so that you can discard one
if you get it at a time you can't play it and still be able to play it
later. This is especially important becuase these are the only blood
gain in your deck. The exception is the barrens. Instead of doubling
it, add three other "cycling" cards, maybe fragment, elder library and
dreams of the sphinx. Intercept decks tend to not play many cards, so
cycling masters are key.

> 7 Rotschreck

Good 'ol Rotschreck... You should probably take out some of your damage
prevention and add more rotschreck, because rotschreck stops your
opponent from avoiding going to torpor and also wacks him before he does
damage which you'd need to prevent.
On the other hand, intercept combat generally can't do anything but kill
its predator and make its grandpredator win, so I would strongly suggest
that you make an intercept-s:ce deck, in which case you'd want to take
out all of the rotschrecks.

> Minion cards
>
> 1 Mister Wintrop |
> 5 Sport Bike | 12
> 2 Raven Spy |

Good, good, permanent intercept. Very important to the endgame, which
this deck tends to get to after prolonging the game.

> 2 Crimson Sentinel |
> 2 Bang Nakh |

Weapons are bad in general and are even worse if you are using claws
because they don't do agg. Take them out.

> 8 Cat's guidance |
> 6 Rats Warning | 20
> 6 Forced awakening |

Probably need more of all of these. Untapping is key to intercept
strategies because otherwise you can't ever take actions, which equals
death. Cat's guidance is one of the best cards available to this deck,
so 8 is an absolute minimum. Add more.

> 12 Bone Spur |
> 3 Earth Meld |

If you try to include both combat contingencies in your deck, its more
likely that you will have them at the wrong time than the right. Go all
one way or the other, and overall you will come out ahead.

> 12 Rolling with the punches| 33
> 5 Indomitability |
> 1 Canine Horde |

Canine horde is lousy. Take it out. Aid from bats is far superior, but
only in large numbers.

> 7 Forms of the ghost | 10
> 3 Arson |

You have no stealth in this deck, so anytime there's somthing worth
arsoning, the action'll get blocked. Might as well be a bum's rush.

Messages.Author: Lupus Australis
Messages.Body:
On Sun, 7 Mar 1999, Steve Wampler wrote:

> Um... I hate to have to be the one to tell you, but Camille and Raven
> are officially the same card so you really only have two vampires in
> this crypt.

This is, AFAIK, not true at all. Camille Devereaux and Raven are
officially different vampires, for the simple and practical reason that
they have different names.

It is a common house rule that they are the same, based on the logic that
Raven (from V:tES) is a direct and identical replacement of the
discontinued Camille (from Jyhad). Jyhad On Line still keeps a house rule
that they are the same and will contest each other. (Personally, I don't
see the logic in this house rule.)

In spite of their being officially different, it is sometimes illegal to
use them together in tournament play. This is because of the optional
tournament rule that you cannot mix card backs in your crypt. The rule
states that all cards in a crypt must be either all V:tES-backed cards or
all Jyhad-backed cards. Since there is no V:tES-backed Camille, and no
Jyhad-backed Raven, it is legally impossible to have them in the same
crypt when this rule is in force. Even in this case, however, they are
not considered the same vampire, and will not contest eachother if brought
out by different players.

This rule is optional, and according to DCI rules cannot be enforced
unless advance notice was given to players as part of the tournament
announcement. Thus, unless the tournament you wish to play in
specifically announces that you cannot mix card backs in your crypt, it
will be perfectly acceptable to play Camille and Raven together in that
tournament.

LSJ, please confirm if I got all this right.

Lupus Australis

I don't see anything particularly "unfair" about making use of a legal
option that is available to all players. Any advantage gained would be
minimal. Using this advantage does indeed violate the intent of the game
design, but I think it far more unfair to rule that players can only use
half their collection when designing crypts.

> To circumvent this,
> we always use black-shield sleeves. They look good, and you can mix
> VTES and Jyhad without marking the Camille-cards. :)

Well, yes. So do I. I don't like knowing, or anyone else knowing,
anything about my cards before they are played. But I've never been
particularly concerned about the advantage gained by others not using the
sleeves.

But if you are concerned about this problem, I'd like to point out that it
is not limited to Jyhad vs. V:tES. There is also a difference between the
V:tES/DS backs and the AH/Sabbat backs. It is not as obvious, but once
you are aware, it is extremely simple to tell them apart.

> option that is available to all players. Any advantage gained would be
> minimal. Using this advantage does indeed violate the intent of the game
> design, but I think it far more unfair to rule that players can only use
> half their collection when designing crypts.

While it is legal to mix card backs when playing without the optional
rule, it is not legal to mark cards, manipulate which cards are drawn
from your deck, or use card backs as an identifying mark. This, from
the DCI rules:

"All library cards from the Jyhad or Vampire: The Eternal Struggle card
sets must be of sufficiently mixed card type-that is, Master cards must
appear with both Jyhad and V:TES card backs (or at least three different
card types must have Jyhad backs)."

Yes, this rule specifically applies to the library cards, but the DCI's
list of types of cheating says that the provided list is not
exhaustive. I don't think extending this precedent to a crypt is
unreasonable. A player wishing to use Camille and Raven must still
avoid having a marked crypt by adding other Jyhad backed cards.

Messages.Author: Lupus Australis
Messages.Body:
On Mon, 8 Mar 1999, Robert Goudie wrote:

> While it is legal to mix card backs when playing without the optional
> rule, it is not legal to mark cards, manipulate which cards are drawn
> from your deck, or use card backs as an identifying mark. This, from
> the DCI rules:
>
> "All library cards from the Jyhad or Vampire: The Eternal Struggle card
> sets must be of sufficiently mixed card type-that is, Master cards must
> appear with both Jyhad and V:TES card backs (or at least three different
> card types must have Jyhad backs)."
>

> Yes, this rule specifically applies to the library cards, but the DCI's
> list of types of cheating says that the provided list is not
> exhaustive. I don't think extending this precedent to a crypt is
> unreasonable. A player wishing to use Camille and Raven must still
> avoid having a marked crypt by adding other Jyhad backed cards.

I agree in principle that players should not try to specifically design
their crypts in order to maximize knowledge derived from differences in
card backs. (I use the opaque card sleeves myself) Nonetheless, if there
are different card backs in the crypt it will be impossible for the player
to *not* know something he shouldn't based on this information.
Maintaining an "appropriate mix" of cards only alleviates this problem
slightly without eliminating it -- especially as relates to the crypt,
where there are only 12 cards to begin with.

So in spite of agreeing in principle, I cannot see how this constitutes a
"rule" since rules must be enforceable to be meaningful. A rule of this
nature is not even self-enforceable, since once you allow yourself the
mix, you cannot prevent yourself from gaining information from the card
backs. And once you have this information, how can you prevent yourself
from gaining advantage from it?

This sort of problem can be handled by handing a player a dozen
black-backed card sleeves before the start of the game. No other method
is particularly reasonable, once you allow mixing at all.

Nor do I see much point in telling players their crypt must be
"appropriately mixed" without specific guidelines as to what is
"appropriate". Since no amount of mixing can eliminate the problem, what
is appropriate is going to be a judgement call. The DCI rules do not
provide any specific rule relative to crypt mixing, so I cannot see that
any rule can be inferred.

There is a rule against playing with marked crypts. This rule is directly
contradicted in principle by specifically allowing a mix of Jyhad and
V:tES, as well as by allowing players to mix V:tES/DS backed cards with
AH/Sabbat backed cards. A tournament judge who is not willing to hand out
opaque card sleeves would do best to just shrug his shoulders and ignore
the issue, as I see no other way to resolve the contradiction.

What would you consider appropriate card mixing in the following case: A
deck using one or more Camille (Jyhad), one or more Raven (V:tES/DS), and
several Gangrel Antitribu (AH/Sabbat). How is one to mix the three
different card-backs approprately to prevent oneself from gaining
knowledge therefrom?

There are a number of rules that are only barely enforceable.
Collusion, for example, will almost never be proven but is still against

will typically have a different mix of card backs than those who intend
to mark their cyrpts.

> What would you consider appropriate card mixing in the following case: A
> deck using one or more Camille (Jyhad), one or more Raven (V:tES/DS), and
> several Gangrel Antitribu (AH/Sabbat). How is one to mix the three
> different card-backs approprately to prevent oneself from gaining
> knowledge therefrom?

If that was a 12 card deck with 4 of each and there are not other Jyhad
versions available of the !Gan or Raven then it is fine.

I agree that this is a mostly theoretical discussion. However, if I see
a player cutting his crypt at the start of a game (the cut that is
allowed right after the player's predator shuffles and/or cuts) and
fanning the cards before he cuts, and I then discover that their the
entire deck is made of Jyhad backed Malks save for Anson who has a V:TES
back, I can see that the player did not make an effort to mix their
crypt and that it was their intent to gain an advantage.

>
> In article <7c2gqd$me2$1...@nnrp1.dejanews.com>,
> <carl.pi...@at.ccmail.philips.com> wrote:
> >I always had the impression that Magic had not such a bad colour choice
> >for the backs as VTES had.
> >But that's not the point. WotC should make sure that something never
> >again happens, it sucks!
> >Btw, how can such a thing happen, is there no quality assurance?
>
> I don't think it's as easy as you guys think. And anyway, it's not
> actually WotC's fault (much as I've come to despise them), but the
> printers, right?

It's not easy at all. Even during the same print run with the same
plates there will be differences. Printers with good quality control
can minimize this effect but can only eliminate it by throwing out a
whole lot of the cards that are outside of an ultra strict tolerance
level.
